title: Amitabha's Primal Vow
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Answer: When Amitabha Buddha was formerly the bhikshu Dharmakara, he made forty-eight great vows to perfect the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss and save all sentient beings. Among them, the Eighteenth Vow is known as the Primal Vow of Amitabha Buddha. (See further the Sutra of Infinite Life Expounded by the Buddha.)

inline.s: Question: What is the Primal Vow of Amitabha Buddha?

Answer: When Amitabha Buddha was formerly the bhikshu Dharmakara, he made forty-eight great vows to perfect the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss and save all sentient beings. Among them, the Eighteenth Vow is known as the Primal Vow of Amitabha Buddha. (See further the Sutra of Infinite Life Expounded by the Buddha.)
Question: What is the Eighteenth Vow?
Answer: In order to broadly save sentient beings in the ten directions, Amitabha Buddha made forty-eight great vows. Among them, the Eighteenth Vow is:

“If I must attain Buddhahood, and sentient beings of the ten directions, with utmost sincerity and joyful faith, wish to be reborn in my land, even down to ten thoughts, and are not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment — save only for those who commit the five deadly offenses and slander the true Dharma.”
(from the Sutra of Infinite Life Expounded by the Buddha)

[The five deadly offenses] Killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, killing an arhat, splitting the harmonious Sangha, and shedding the blood of the Buddha. Because they betray and violate kindness, they are called the five deadly offenses.

Question: Does this “even down to ten thoughts” refer to ten thoughts in daily life, or ten thoughts at the moment of death? The Primal Vow teaching maintains that “recitation of the name necessarily brings rebirth” and moreover opposes spiritual practice, its reasoning being: “The meaning of the Eighteenth Vow (the Primal Vow), the very root of the Pure Land school, is that as long as one recites the Buddha’s name ten times with a scattered mind in daily life (‘even down to ten thoughts’), one will certainly be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss at the moment of death (‘if not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment’).” Is this correct?
Answer: The “even down to ten thoughts” spoken of in the Eighteenth Vow does not refer to daily life,
but to the ten thoughts at the moment of death
First, the Eighteenth Vow was proclaimed by Sakyamuni Buddha in the Sutra of Infinite Life Expounded by the Buddha.
In this sutra,
the Buddha exhorts:
though toiling for a whole lifetime
, in but a moment you will be reborn in the land of Immeasurable Life, with bliss beyond measure.”
At the end of the scripture, the Buddha again earnestly admonishes:
“You should faithfully accept and follow,
practice in accordance with the Dharma
If

“even down to ten thoughts” meant that “as long as one recites the Buddha’s name ten times in daily life, one will certainly be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss,” why would the Buddha exhort “
though toiling for a whole lifetime
”? And why, at the end, would the Buddha admonish “
practice in accordance with the Dharma

”? The Primal Vow teaching, following their distortion of “even down to ten thoughts,” maintains that “recitation of the name necessarily brings rebirth — one need not observe precepts, need not do good, need not purify one’s own mind, and even committing evil throughout one’s life is of no consequence” and the doctrine of “the evil person as the proper object [of salvation]” (see
“The Primal Vow Teaching Is an Outwardly-Buddhist Heresy”
, in that article), and moreover opposes spiritual practice — this is very wrong.
The Buddha says
“practice in accordance with the Dharma”
, yet they oppose spiritual practice — this is to stand in direct opposition to the Buddha.
Second, the Sutra of Praise of the Pure Land and Acceptance by the Buddha

is praised and accepted by all the Buddhas of the ten directions (of course including Amitabha Buddha of the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss). Our master Sakyamuni Buddha clearly instructs in the sutra:

“If there are pure-faith good men or good women who hear this name of Amitayus Buddha — immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable in its meritorious virtue — and the meritorious adornments of the Land of Ultimate Bliss; and, having heard, reflect upon it, whether for a day and a night, or two or three, or four or five, or six or seven [days and nights],
with single-minded recollection undisturbed
— this
(this)
good man or good woman, at the moment of death, with Amitayus Buddha together with his countless sravaka disciples and assemblies of bodhisattvas, surrounding him before and behind,
comes and stands before him
, and with compassion and safeguarding
, makes his mind not disturbed. Having given up this life, he follows the Buddha’s assembly and is reborn in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitayus.”

Therefore, the requirement for certain rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is: single-minded recollection undisturbed. Precisely because one has attained single-minded recollection undisturbed in daily life, one can ensure the accomplishment of the ten thoughts at the moment of death, and thus be decisively reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. If, in the Sutra of Infinite Life Expounded by the Buddha, the “even down to ten thoughts” of the Eighteenth Vow refers to ten thoughts in daily life,

, then why would our master Sakyamuni Buddha still speak of “single-minded recollection undisturbed, …, and be reborn in that Buddha-land”? Why would he, again and again and again in the sutra, admonish to “practice as taught,” and earnestly warn to “give rise to no doubt” and to “practice no indulgence”? Moreover, this instruction
is praised and accepted by all the Buddhas of the ten directions (of course including Amitabha Buddha) — why is this so?
(See further
“Sutra of Praise of the Pure Land and Acceptance by the Buddha”
Therefore, this proves that
the “even down to ten thoughts” of the Eighteenth Vow is not ten thoughts in daily life, but ten thoughts at the moment of death.
Third, Master Shandao is the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha

. Regarding Master Shandao, Master Yinguang — the manifestation of Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva — praised him: “Master Shandao is the incarnation of Amitabha Buddha, with great transcendental powers and great wisdom.” (From the Collected Essays of Master Yinguang
Reply to the Brothers of Layman Xu Yongjia.) So, what Master Shandao says is equivalent to what Amitabha Buddha himself proclaimed.
Master Shandao instructed:
“If, at the approach of the end of a grave illness, the relatives must not shed tears and weep, nor raise sounds of sighing and regret, which would disturb the patient’s mind, and
cause him to lose right mindfulness
. But let them recite the Buddha’s name together with one voice; only when the breath has ceased may they weep.
If there is the least attachment to the world in his heart, it becomes an obstruction, and he cannot be liberated.
If there is someone who understands the Pure Land and comes often to encourage him, that is a great fortune. If one acts according to this, he will certainly be reborn beyond, without doubt.”
See further
“Annotation to Master Shandao’s Essay on Right Mindfulness and Rebirth at Death”
) In this Essay on Right Mindfulness and Rebirth at Death, Master Shandao continues to instruct:

This method — practiced by monks, laypeople, and even those who have never recitated, — all are reborn, without any doubt. I have seen many in the world who, in ordinary daily life, recitate the Buddha’s name, praise and bow, and vow to be reborn in the West, with great
earnestness and sincerity
. Yet when illness comes, they are afraid of death, and speak no more of rebirth and liberation. Only when their breath has faded and life ended,
and their consciousness has entered the dark realm
, do they at last recite ten thoughts. This is exactly like closing the door after the thief has gone — of what use is it? Birth and death are a great matter;
one must exert one’s own strength
to succeed.
If there be a single thought-moment of error, and one suffers for many kalpas
, who can take your place? Think on this! Think on this! When one is free of illness, one should take up this method
with earnest diligence
, for this is
the great matter of the final hour

Master Shandao is the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, and his instruction on “right mindfulness at death” proves that the “even down to ten thoughts” of the Eighteenth Vow is ten thoughts at the moment of death. For if the “even down to ten thoughts” of the Eighteenth Vow were ten thoughts in daily life, why would Master Shandao, the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, still need to speak of “right mindfulness at death”? Moreover, throughout his life Master Shandao vigorously promoted the upholding of the Amitabha Sutra Expounded by the Buddha, personally writing out more than one hundred thousand scrolls and distributing them to his disciples and followers, telling them to practice as taught: with a single undivided mind, the Buddha will surely come to welcome. If ten thoughts in daily life sufficed for rebirth, why would Master Shandao write out more than one hundred thousand scrolls of the Amitabha Sutra for his disciples and followers? It would have been enough to write out the four characters ‘ten thoughts bring rebirth’ or ‘recitation of the name necessarily brings rebirth.’
From this it is proven that the “even down to ten thoughts” of the Eighteenth Vow is not ten thoughts in daily life, but ten thoughts at the moment of death.

Fourth, Master Yongming is the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, and therefore Master Yongming’s birthday, the seventeenth day of the eleventh lunar month, has been observed as the anniversary of Amitabha Buddha’s enlightenment.

Regarding Master Yongming, Master Yinguang — the manifestation of Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva — praised him: “Master Yongming is the incarnation of Amitabha Buddha. With great compassion and great pity, he teaches and transforms sentient beings.” (From the Collected Essays of Master Yinguang
Dharma Talk at the World Buddhist Laymen’s Grove.) So, what Master Yongming says is equivalent to what Amitabha Buddha himself proclaimed.
Master Yongming instructed:
“When walking within the Way
(circumambulation)
, or when bowing in reverence, or when reciting the Buddha’s name and making vows, with bitter toil and utmost sincerity,
free of any different thought,
as if going to execution, as if within the bi-lao
(bi-lao: a prison)

, pursued by enemies and thieves, pressed by fire and water, earnestly seeking deliverance, wishing to escape the wheel of suffering, swiftly to realize the unborn, broadly to save all conscious beings, to continue and exalt the Triple Gem, vowing to repay the four kindnesses — with such sincerity, the merit will not be lost. If speech and conduct do not correspond,
(speech and conduct not matching)
, with weak strength of faith, without
a mind of thought-after-thought continuity,
and a will to break off again and again
(the mindful thought of recitation broken off by deluded thoughts)
, relying upon this negligence, at the final hour hoping for rebirth, he is but obstructed by karmic hindrances, and in fear will be unable to meet his good friend
(for fear he will not meet a spiritual friend who can accomplish his right mindfulness at death)
; the winds and fire press upon him, and right mindfulness is not accomplished
(not able to accomplish right mindfulness at death, and hence not reborn)
. Why is this?
The present is the cause and the final hour is the fruit;
so the cause must be real, and the fruit will then not be empty. If one wishes
the ten thoughts at death to be accomplished,
he should but prepare the ferry and the bridge in advance, gather together merit, and dedicate it to that hour
(dedicating to the moment of death)
, thought after thought without lapse
(accomplishing thought-after-thought continuity)
; then there is nothing to fear.”
(from the Collected Essays on the Common Return of All Good Deeds)

[Speech and conduct not corresponding] Speech and conduct do not match. In words one says one truly believes and sincerely vows, but in actual action the faith is not genuine and the vow not sincere: shrinking from hardship and pain, being lazy and lax. Hence Master Yongming’s next sentence is:
“Weak is the strength of faith.”
And he rebukes, saying:
“Relying upon this negligence.”
Those who recite the Buddha’s name should keep firmly in mind the earnest teaching of the Buddha in the Sutra of Immeasurable Life:
though toiling for a whole lifetime
, in but a moment you will be reborn in the land of Immeasurable Life,
with bliss beyond measure
[The ten thoughts at the moment of death accomplished] Accomplishing the ten thoughts of continual recitation at the moment of death.
[Preparing the ferry and the bridge] “Ferry and bridge”: a crossing and a bridge. “Preparing the ferry and the bridge” means making preparation in advance.
Master Yongming is the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, and his instruction on “the ten thoughts at death being accomplished”
proves that the “even down to ten thoughts” of the Eighteenth Vow is not ten thoughts in daily life, but ten thoughts at the moment of death
. For if the “even down to ten thoughts” of the Eighteenth Vow were ten thoughts in daily life, why would Master Yongming, the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, still need to speak of “
the ten thoughts at death being accomplished

The final decision at the moment of death is the true decision. At the moment of death, it is like a person arriving at an airport: in daily life he said he would go here, then there — but where he ultimately goes depends entirely on which airplane he finally boards (even if in a daze, it is he himself who boards). This is the final vow, the final decision. Therefore,
the accomplishment of the ten thoughts at the moment of death is extremely crucial
Conclusion One: From this we know, the “even down to ten thoughts” of the Eighteenth Vow
is ten thoughts at the moment of death

Question: Does “the ten thoughts at death attain rebirth” mean that, as long as one recites the Buddha’s name for ten thought-moments at the moment of death, one will certainly be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss?
Answer: These ten thoughts are
the utmost sincerity
of the ten thoughts (
“with utmost sincerity and joyful faith”
Utmost sincerity means the mind-thought is pure and single, without any mixture.
Therefore the ten thoughts of utmost sincerity
are the ten thoughts of recitation whose mindful thought continues thought after thought (ten recitations of the Buddha’s name without a single deluded thought).
“The ten thoughts at death attain rebirth,” concretely, means: the ten thoughts of continual recitation at death decide rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Hence the ten thoughts of continual recitation at death (ten recitations of the Buddha’s name without a single deluded thought) — these are the ten thoughts spoken of in the Eighteenth Vow:
“with utmost sincerity and joyful faith, wishing to be reborn in my land, even down to ten thoughts”
Utmost sincerity means pure and single, undivided

. If at this crucial moment, while reciting, one still mixes in other thoughts, one cannot be said to have “utmost sincerity and joyful faith, wishing to be reborn in my land”; how could one then be in sympathetic resonance with Amitabha Buddha? Master Yinguang said:

“The minds of sentient beings are like water; Amitabha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings are complete in faith and vow, and with utmost sincerity sense the Buddha, the Buddha responds — just as when the water is clear the moon appears. If the mind is not pure and not utterly sincere, but accords with greed, anger, and delusion, going against the Buddha, it is like turbid, moving water: though the moon does not withhold its shining, it cannot be clearly reflected.”
(from the Collected Essays of Master Yinguang, Preface to the Guide to Pure Land Practice for Beginners)
This is what Master Shandao called “
unbroken thought brings rebirth
” — that is, what Master Yongming called “
the ten thoughts at death being accomplished

” (before speaking of “the ten thoughts at death being accomplished,” Master Yongming had already spoken of “free of any different thought” and “a mind of thought-after-thought continuity”; see the quotation above). That is, what Master Yinguang called “
apart from this thought, utterly no other thought
”. Master Yinguang said:
“In the Contemplation Sutra, one who has committed the five deadly offenses and the ten evil deeds, when about to die, sees the signs of the hells appear. If there is a good spiritual friend
(original note: here it does not matter whether monk or layman, man or woman; whoever can teach him to recite the Buddha’s name is called a good spiritual friend.)

who teaches him to recite the Buddha’s name, even if he recites only ten sounds, or fewer than ten sounds, and directly dies, he, too, relying on the Buddha’s compassionate power, is reborn while still bearing his karma. These ten thoughts, compared with ordinary ten thoughts, have a force of intensity as different as heaven from the abyss, and so he attains rebirth. Pressed by the extreme suffering of hell, the moment he hears the Buddha’s name he recites it with his whole being.
Apart from this thought, utterly no other thought
Though he has not personally realized one mind undisturbed, yet his mind is ultimately without any different thought.
(from the Collected Essays of Master Yinguang, Third Compilation
Volume Two
Reply to Layman Chen Xinru.) The Two Gates of Resolving Doubts and of Practice and Vow for Rebirth in the Pure Land says:
“Though originally one of evil and offense,
with ten thoughts of utmost sincerity
, he is reborn in that land.”
Therefore,
in order to ensure the ten thoughts of continual recitation at the moment of death,
Master Shandao earnestly admonishes:
Precisely because recitation of the name is easy
precisely because name-recitation is easier to accomplish than visual-contemplation recitation
unbroken thought brings rebirth
If one can
continue thought after thought

, to the end of life, then of ten, ten are reborn, and of a hundred, a hundred are reborn......May all people reflect well within themselves: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse the mind, restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing.”
For the detailed content of Master Shandao’s instruction on “unbroken thought brings rebirth,” see
“Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teaching”
, in that article.
[Unbroken thought brings rebirth]
“Unbroken thought brings rebirth” means:
at the moment of death, the mindful thought of recitation unbroken
(not broken by deluded thoughts)
, and he attains rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Here “unbroken” means the mindful thought of recitation continuing thought after thought, with no deluded thought mixed in (if a deluded thought is mixed in, it is not unbroken). One must never misunderstand the word “unbroken” here as the Buddha’s name continuing on the lips (while deluded thoughts are mixed in the mind). This is what is meant by “a hair’s breadth of error leads a thousand li astray.” [Thought after thought continuing, to the end of life] Because, at the moment of death, unbroken mindful thought of recitation brings rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, one should thus practice for one’s whole life,
making the mindful thought of recitation continue and form into a habit

. Then one will certainly be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss — of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn. [Formed into a habit] Through constant repeated practice, making the mindful thought of recitation continue and become an instinct.

[Rousing the mind, restraining oneself] Rousing the mind, stirring up the mind to do what should be done; restraining oneself, constraining oneself from doing what should not be done. The four characters “rousing the mind, restraining oneself” are a powerful weapon for overcoming difficulties and sweeping away obstacles.
[Day and night never ceasing] Not stopping the thought-after-thought continuity day or night.
In order to ensure the ten thoughts of continual recitation at the moment of death,
Master Yongming instructed:
“When walking within the Way
(circumambulation)
, or when bowing in reverence, or when reciting the Buddha’s name and making vows, with bitter toil and utmost sincerity,
free of any different thought,
as if going to execution, as if within the bi-lao
(bi-lao: a prison)

, pursued by enemies and thieves, pressed by fire and water, earnestly seeking deliverance, wishing to escape the wheel of suffering, swiftly to realize the unborn, broadly to save all conscious beings, to continue and exalt the Triple Gem, vowing to repay the four kindnesses — with such sincerity, the merit will not be lost. If speech and conduct do not correspond, with weak strength of faith, without
a mind of thought-after-thought continuity,
and a will to break off again and again
(the mindful thought of recitation broken off by deluded thoughts)
, relying upon this negligence, at the final hour hoping for rebirth, he is but obstructed by karmic hindrances, and in fear will be unable to meet his good friend
(for fear he will not meet a spiritual friend who can arouse his right mindfulness at death)
; the winds and fire press upon him, and right mindfulness is not accomplished. Why is this?
The present is the cause and the final hour is the fruit;
so the cause must be real, and the fruit will then not be empty. If one wishes
the ten thoughts at death to be accomplished,
he should but prepare the ferry and the bridge in advance, gather together merit, and dedicate it to that hour
(dedicating to the moment of death)
, thought after thought without lapse
(accomplishing thought-after-thought continuity)
; then there is nothing to fear.”
(from the Collected Essays on the Common Return of All Good Deeds)
Please note that Master Yongming says: if it is

“without a mind of thought-after-thought continuity, and a will to break off again and again,” then rebirth is hard to attain. Therefore, what Master Yongming calls “the ten thoughts at death being accomplished” means accomplishing the ten thoughts of continual recitation at the moment of death. “Dedicating to that hour” means dedicating to the moment of death; “thought after thought without lapse” means continuing thought after thought without break. Hence, “dedicating to that hour, thought after thought without lapse” means dedicating to the moment of death continual thought-after-thought continuity. So then, “there is nothing to fear” (i.e., one is thus able to be assured of rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss).
On this, Master Daochuo also instructed in the Collected Essays on the Peaceful Grove:
For all sentient beings, at the moment of death
, the knife-wind severs the body, the suffering of death presses upon them, and great terror arises. Therefore, meeting a good spiritual friend, they rouse great bravery,
and recite ten thoughts with mind after mind continuing
, and this is a superior root of goodness,
and they attain rebirth
Please note that here Master Daochuo teaches: for all sentient beings, at the moment of death, ten thoughts with mind after mind continuing, and they attain rebirth. That is:
ten thoughts at the moment of death, unbroken thought brings rebirth.

[Knife-wind] When a person is dying, he fully experiences the suffering of death, and the four great elements separate. Among these, the wind that severs the limbs and joints like a knife is called the “knife-wind.” The Sutra of Right Dharma Mindfulness says: “At the end of life, the knife-winds all stir, and the skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, fat, essence, and blood are all cut and severed.” The Sutra of the Five Kings says: “When about to die, the knife-wind severs the body, and there is no place without pain.”
Therefore, regarding the meaning of the Eighteenth Vow, Master Daochuo clearly instructs in the Collected Essays on the Peaceful Grove:
“If there are sentient beings who, even having committed evil all their lives, at the moment of death
recite for ten thoughts continually,
calling upon my name,
and are not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”
Here, Master Daochuo has given a precise explanation of the meaning of “even down to ten thoughts” in the Eighteenth Vow:
at the moment of death, ten thoughts continually, calling upon my name.
Therefore, the “even down to ten thoughts” of the Eighteenth Vow is the ten thoughts at death, and moreover the ten thoughts that continue without break.
Conclusion Two: From this we know, the “even down to ten thoughts” of the Eighteenth Vow
is
the ten thoughts at death that continue thought after thought
Regarding
the ten thoughts of continual recitation at death, Master Daochuo, in the Collected Essays on the Peaceful Grove, has another very important instruction, now transcribed and annotated below:

[Question: The Great Sutra of Immeasurable Life says: “Sentient beings of the ten directions, with utmost sincerity and joyful faith, wishing to be reborn in my land, even down to ten thoughts, and if not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.” Now there are people in the world who, hearing this sage teaching, in this present life pay no attention to it, and intend only at the moment of death to apply their recitation. What about this?]

Question: The Sutra of Immeasurable Life says: “Sentient beings of the ten directions, with utmost sincerity and joyful faith, wishing to be reborn in my land, even down to ten thoughts, and if not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.” Now there are people who, hearing this sage teaching, behave as if paying no attention, and plan only at the moment of death to accomplish the ten thoughts of continual recitation. Pray tell, what do you think of this plan?
[Answer: This plan is not fitting. Why? The sutra speaks of “
ten thoughts continually

,” which seems not difficult. Yet all ordinary beings have minds like wild horses, consciousness more restless than apes, galloping among the six sense-objects — when have they ever rested? Each must arouse faith and prepare by restraining his thoughts in advance,
so as to form them into a habit

, and so make his root of goodness firm. As the Buddha told the great king: “If a person accumulates good acts, he will have no evil thought at death; just as a tree that has first leaned over must, when it falls, follow the bent direction.” If the knife-wind arrives, and a hundred sufferings join in the body, and the practice was not there beforehand, how could the recollection he wishes to achieve be carried out
(be accomplished)

Answer: This plan is to dig a well when already thirsty. Digging a well when thirsty and preparing the ferry and the bridge in advance are two different matters (this is not fitting). Why? The sutra says “ten thoughts continually,” which seems not difficult (hence many people think they will be able to do it at the moment of death). Yet all ordinary beings have minds like wild horses, consciousness more restless than apes, galloping among the six sense-objects (sight, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects) — when have they ever rested? Each must arouse a mind of one-mind faith and prepare by training his thought to be single and his ten thoughts continual, so that it forms into a habit (through constant practice, making the thought single and the ten thoughts continual become an instinct), and only then, at the moment of death, will his root of goodness be firm. As the Buddha told the great king: “If people constantly accumulate good acts, then at death they will have no evil thought; just as when a tree falls over, it must fall toward the direction in which it was already leaning.” If the knife-wind of death arrives and a hundred sufferings press and scorch, and beforehand one has not accomplished the ten thoughts of continual recitation formed into a habit, then at the moment of death, relying only on the wish to achieve “ten thoughts continually” — how could one possibly do it?

[Consciousness more restless than apes] The six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness) are even more unsettled than a monkey that leaps and scrambles wildly. [Formed into a habit] Through repeated practice, making it become an instinct.

[Each should, with three or five companions of like mind, agree beforehand in words, that at the moment of death they will alternately awaken and instruct one another, reciting the name of Amitabha for the dying person and encouraging him to be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss, voice following voice, so as to accomplish the ten thoughts. It is like a wax seal stamped into clay: the seal is destroyed and the inscription is formed. When this life is cut off, that is the moment of rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss. Once one enters the class of the rightly fixed, what is there still to worry about? Each should weigh this great benefit — why not prepare the ten thoughts in advance?]

Therefore, it is best for everyone to invite three or five companions of like mind and agree beforehand: at the moment of death, they will alternately awaken and instruct, reciting the name of Amitabha Buddha for the dying one, encouraging him to firmly fix his vow of rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, voice following voice, so as to accomplish the ten thoughts of continual recitation at death. It is like
a wax seal stamped into clay: though the seal is destroyed, the inscription is already formed;

so when the breath is cut off, that is the moment of rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Once one reaches the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, at once he enters the class of the rightly fixed — and at that time, what is there still to worry about? Each of you must weigh this great benefit: why not prepare in advance the ten thoughts of continual recitation?
[In succession] following one after another. [A wax seal stamped into clay,
the seal
destroyed
and the inscription (
the pattern
) is formed] A wax seal carved with a pattern is pressed onto a clay mold. Heated and dried, when the wax melts, the pattern on the clay mold is formed. The clay mold is used to cast metal vessels.
The Nirvana Sutra says:
“Like a wax seal stamped into clay, the seal and the clay unite; the seal disappears and the inscription is formed.”

Here “the seal destroyed and the inscription formed” is a metaphor for using our physical body to practice, accomplishing the ten thoughts of continual recitation at death; when the breathing stops, though the physical body dies (the seal is destroyed), the great matter of rebirth is at the same time accomplished (the inscription is formed) — “when this life is cut off, that is the moment of rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss.” [The class of the rightly fixed] One of the three classes. [Three classes] The three classes are three types of sentient beings. These three classes are: the class of the rightly fixed, the class of the wrongly fixed, and the class of the unfixed. The class of the rightly fixed refers to the type of sentient beings who will certainly realize enlightenment; the class of the wrongly fixed refers to the type who will ultimately never realize it; the class of the unfixed refers to the type who lies between right and wrong, possibly realizing and possibly not realizing. [Why not prepare the ten thoughts in advance?] Why not train in advance the ten thoughts of continual recitation? This is what Master Yongming, in the passage above, called “preparing the ferry and the bridge.”
Master Daochuo, in the Collected Essays on the Peaceful Grove, has two further very important instructions on rebirth through recitation:
[Even if one has committed evil throughout a whole life,
if only he can bind his mind in single-minded focus
, and constantly recitate the Buddha’s name, all obstructions will naturally be removed, and he will certainly attain rebirth.]
This passage says: even if one has committed evil throughout a whole life,
yet after repentance and turning,
if he can
bind his mind in single-minded focus
(pure thought following in succession), and often recitate the Buddha’s name, then all obstructions are naturally removed, and he will certainly attain rebirth.

Please note: “Even if one has committed evil throughout a whole life” is the situation before repentance; “if only he can bind his mind in single-minded focus, and constantly recitate the Buddha’s name” is the situation after repentance. For if there is no sincere repentance, how could one accomplish binding his mind in single-minded focus?

[From the utmost of a whole life down to ten thoughts, all are reborn. The moment one reaches that land, he enters the class of the rightly fixed — equal in merit to practicing the Way for ten thousand kalpas!]

From the utmost of a whole life of thought-after-thought continuity, down to the ten thoughts of continual recitation at death, all are reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. The moment one reaches the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, he enters the class of the rightly fixed — this is equal in merit to the effect of practicing the Way by the ordinary path for ten thousand kalpas!

[From the utmost of a whole life down to ten thoughts] Viewed from the whole of the Collected Essays on the Peaceful Grove, the meaning is: from the utmost of a whole life of thought-after-thought continuity, down to the ten thoughts of continual recitation at death. The ancients, in writing, prized concision, so when understanding it one must link the preceding and following passages together — never infer meaning from the words alone, nor take a passage out of context.

We read sutras, and the treatises, teachings, and instructions of the patriarchs and great masters, in order to seek the truth. Therefore, one must act from a true and sincere mind: whatever a thing is, that is what it is. Never, for the sake of one’s own selfish ends, play the trick of quoting out of context — for example, distorting “from the utmost of a whole life down to ten thoughts, all are reborn” into: “Master Daochuo says that so long as one recites the Buddha’s name ten times with a scattered mind in daily life (‘down to ten thoughts’), one will certainly be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss at the moment of death (‘all are reborn’). Therefore, recitation of the name necessarily brings rebirth.” The fact is that in the line preceding “from the utmost of a whole life down to ten thoughts, all are reborn,” Master Daochuo had already stated with complete clarity “
if only one can bind his mind in single-minded focus

.” Read the two lines together, then, and “down to ten thoughts” means ten thoughts at the moment of death with the mind bound in single-minded focus (pure thought following in succession) — not ten thoughts recited with a scattered mind in daily life. To quote out of context in this way not only misleads others but also harms oneself.

For another example, they claim that the ‘Passage on Grasping the Vow’s Meaning’ in Master Shandao’s Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra states: “If I attain Buddhahood, and sentient beings of the ten directions call upon my name and aspire to be reborn in my land, down to ten thoughts — if they are not reborn there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.” The meaning, they say, is this: “So long as one recites the Buddha’s name ten times with a scattered mind in daily life (‘down to ten thoughts’), one will certainly be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss at the moment of death (‘if they are not reborn there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment’). Therefore, recitation of the name necessarily brings rebirth.” This is to tear the passage entirely out of context! Anyone who understands Master Shandao’s Pure Land teaching
will know that the “down to ten thoughts” he speaks of is the ten thoughts sustained without break at the moment of death
. Master Shandao earnestly admonished: “
Precisely because recitation of the name is easy
(precisely because name-recitation is easier than visual contemplation)
unbroken thought brings rebirth
If one can
continue thought after thought
, to the end of life
, then of ten, ten are reborn, and of a hundred, a hundred are reborn......May all people reflect well within themselves: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing
.” (see
Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teaching
and
Master Shandao: Unbroken Thought Brings Rebirth
) To quote out of context in this way not only misleads others but also harms oneself.
Master Daochuo further taught in the Collected Essays on the Peaceful Grove:

[Admonishing all sentient beings that they must ever keep the mindful thought present before them, the verse says: In prime of life, when ills are none, the slothful leave the path undone; they grasp at worldly tasks for gain, nor giving, precepts, meditation train. Then death devours them, and they weep for good they never thought to reap. The wise should watch with inward eye and cut the five desires’ tie. Who trains his mind with diligence at life’s end knows no vain repentance. When mind is fixed and wholly one, confused and erring thoughts are gone.
The wise man diligently reins his mind, and leaves no scattered thought behind. Who never trained his mind to stay will find his thoughts at death give way.
A scattered mind is like a horse trained at the mill to walk its course; in battle it but wheels and turns, and straight ahead it never learns.]

This is an admonition to all sentient beings that they must surely keep the mindful thought constantly present. The verse says: in the prime of youth, when one’s strength is full, if one is indolent and not diligent, greedily busying oneself with all manner of affairs and not cultivating giving, precepts, or meditation, then when the end of life comes and one repents, wishing to cultivate wholesome deeds, it will be too late (the wholesome deeds spoken of here are the “giving, precepts, and meditation” mentioned above — giving, the precepts, and meditation). A wise person should be good at observing his own thoughts, so as to cut off the delusions of the five desires. One who thus diligently practices and concentrates the mind single-mindedly will have no regret at death, for since the mind has already become single-minded and fixed in its nature, there will be no confused thoughts at the hour of death. The wise, through their diligent practice in gathering the mind during daily life, will not have a scattered mind at death. But one who does not practice concentrating the mind in daily life will surely have a scattered mind at death. And at that time, if the mind is scattered, you cannot make it single even if you wish: this is just like training a horse by making it pull a mill in daily life, so that in battle the horse will only run in circles and never charge straight ahead.

[The five desires] 1. Form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. Form refers to beautiful appearance; sound refers to melodious tones; fragrance refers to pleasant scents; taste refers to delicious flavors; and touch refers to agreeable sensations. Because these five are able to give rise to a mind of craving, they are called the five desires. 2. The desire for wealth, for lust, for fame, for food and drink, and for sleep. The sutra says: “Wealth, lust, fame, food, and sleep — the five roots of hell.” [Like training a horse at a mill] It is like training a horse by making it pull a mill. “wèi,” a stone mill.

Question: What are the similarities and differences, and what is the relation, between the ten thoughts of continual recitation at death and the single-minded recollection undisturbed spoken of in the Amitabha Sutra Expounded by the Buddha?

Answer: The ten thoughts of continual recitation at death speak of the moment of death, whereas the single-minded recollection undisturbed spoken of in the Amitabha Sutra Expounded by the Buddha refers to daily life (see in detail
Single-Minded Recollection Undisturbed

). The relation between the two is this: single-minded recollection undisturbed in daily life is the most reliable guarantee of the ten thoughts of continual recitation at death — as the saying goes, “Train an army for a thousand days, to use it for a single hour.” On this, Master Daochuo gives a vivid analogy: a warhorse must be given real battle training in daily life. If in daily life it is trained by making it pull a mill, then in battle it will only run in circles and cannot charge into the enemy ranks. (Master Daochuo’s original words:

“The wise man diligently reins his mind, and leaves no scattered thought behind. Who never trained his mind to stay will find his thoughts at death give way. A scattered mind is like a horse trained at the mill to walk its course
(wèi, a millstone)
. In battle it but wheels and turns, and straight ahead it never learns.”
Question: Why is it said that reciting the name of the Buddha is “the extremely easy path”?

Answer: In the practice of Buddha-recitation, one need only accomplish visual contemplation, or the ten thoughts of continual recitation at death, to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, end birth and death, and escape the round of rebirth. Compared with the ordinary paths of practice, which require cutting off afflictions before one can end birth and death and escape the round of rebirth, this is easier by far; therefore
the practice of Buddha-recitation is the easy path
. And compared with accomplishing visual contemplation, the ten thoughts of continual recitation at death are easier still; therefore
reciting the name of the Buddha is the extremely easy path

. So it may be said: those who cut off afflictions are as rare as phoenix feathers and unicorn horns, and those who accomplish visual contemplation are likewise rare and hard to find; but the ten thoughts of continual recitation at death can be accomplished by everyone through unremitting effort. Master Shandao says:
“Sentient beings are heavy with hindrances, the object is subtle while the mind is coarse, consciousness surges and the spirit flies, so contemplation is hard to accomplish
(visual contemplation is hard to accomplish)
. Therefore the great sage, out of compassion
(that is, Sakyamuni Buddha out of compassion)
, directly urges one to call the name exclusively. Precisely because recitation of the name is easy
(precisely because name-recitation is easier than visual contemplation)
unbroken thought brings rebirth
. If one can continue thought after thought, to the end of life, then of ten, ten are reborn, and of a hundred, a hundred are reborn.”
(from On Exclusive and Mixed Practice of Pure Karma)
[Visual contemplation] This refers to the thirteen contemplations in the Contemplation Sutra of Immeasurable Life, such as the contemplation of the sun and the contemplation of water.
Question: Are the ten thoughts of continual recitation at death very difficult? How can one accomplish the ten thoughts of continual recitation at death?

Answer: The ten thoughts of continual recitation at death can be attained by everyone through unremitting effort; it is a Dharma gate in which ten thousand practice and ten thousand go. As for how one can accomplish the ten thoughts of continual recitation at death, see in detail
The Ten Thoughts at Death: Unbroken Thought Brings Rebirth
in that article.
Question:

For the Eighteenth Vow (the Primal Vow), the very root of the Pure Land school, Master Shandao — the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha — gives a very concise and lucid explanation (called the ‘Passage on Grasping the Vow’s Meaning’),
set out as follows
The ‘Passage on Grasping the Vow’s Meaning’ in Master Shandao’s Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra
says
If I attain Buddhahood, and sentient beings of the ten directions call upon my name and aspire to be reborn in my land
, down to ten thoughts
— if they are not reborn there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The ‘Passage on Grasping the Vow’s Meaning’ in Master Shandao’s Dharma-Door of Contemplation and Mindfulness
says
If I become a Buddha, and sentient beings of the ten directions, aspiring to be reborn in my land, call upon my name
, down to ten sounds
, riding upon the power of my vow — if they are not reborn there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The ‘Passage on Grasping the Vow’s Meaning’ in Master Shandao’s Rites of Praise for Rebirth
says
If I become a Buddha, and sentient beings of the ten directions call upon my name
, down to ten sounds

— if they are not reborn there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. That Buddha now appears, having become a Buddha in this world; know that this primal pledge, this weighty vow, is not in vain: sentient beings who recite will certainly attain rebirth.

In these three ‘Passages on Grasping the Vow’s Meaning,’ all say that by “down to ten thoughts” or “down to ten sounds” one will certainly attain rebirth. That is to say: so long as one recites the Buddha’s name ten times with a scattered mind in daily life, one will certainly be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss at the moment of death. Therefore Master Shandao says: recitation of the name necessarily brings rebirth. Is that not so?
Answer: The ancients prized concision in their writing; therefore, when understanding a passage, one must link the preceding and following text
, together with the author’s overall thought,
and consider them together — never inferring meaning from the words alone, nor taking a passage out of context.
In the age of Master Shandao (
), because of a series of teachings given by Master Daochuo (
the “even down to ten thoughts” of the Eighteenth Vow had already become an undisputed consensus to mean the ten thoughts sustained without break at the moment of death
, so that whenever “even down to ten thoughts,” “down to ten thoughts,” or “down to ten sounds” was spoken of,
everyone knew that what was meant was the ten thoughts sustained without break at the moment of death
, and so in writing they no longer belabored the point. As for the meaning of the Eighteenth Vow, Master Daochuo has already explained it very clearly in the Collected Essays on the Peaceful Grove:
If there are sentient beings who, even having committed evil all their lives,
at the moment of death recite ten thoughts without break,
calling upon my name — if they are not reborn there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”
Here Master Daochuo has given a precise explanation of the meaning of “even down to ten thoughts” in the Eighteenth Vow:
at the moment of death, ten thoughts without break.
And as set forth above, Master Daochuo gave a whole series of teachings on the ten thoughts of continual recitation at death. Master Shandao himself also stated plainly:
unbroken thought brings rebirth
. Master Shandao says:
“Precisely because recitation of the name is easy
(precisely because name-recitation is easier than visual contemplation)
unbroken thought brings rebirth
If one can continue thought after thought, to the end of life
, then of ten, ten are reborn, and of a hundred, a hundred are reborn.
May all people reflect well within themselves:
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing

(If Master Shandao advocated “recitation of the name necessarily brings rebirth,” why did he still say “continue thought after thought, to the end of life” and “whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing”? Since the Primal Vow teaching claims to rely on Master Shandao, why do you not follow Master Shandao’s teaching “
continue thought after thought, to the end of life
” and “
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing
”? Instead you preach that no practice is needed. Is it truly that no practice is needed? Read Master Shandao’s teachings and instructions carefully!)
(see
Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teaching
and
Master Shandao: Unbroken Thought Brings Rebirth
What is more, Master Shandao also specially wrote the Essay on Right Mindfulness and Rebirth at Death, in order to emphasize
that right mindfulness at the moment of death brings rebirth
(see
Master Shandao’s Essay on Right Mindfulness and Rebirth at Death (Annotated)

). Ignoring these facts, the Primal Vow teaching twists Master Shandao’s “down to ten thoughts” and “down to ten sounds” into reciting the Buddha’s name ten times with a scattered mind in daily life, and concludes from this that Master Shandao said recitation of the name necessarily brings rebirth. Yet in fact Master Shandao plainly taught
“unbroken thought brings rebirth”
and
“right mindfulness at the moment of death brings rebirth”

. How can one so wantonly distort the facts? In studying the Dharma, one must act from a true and sincere mind. The saying goes: “To cover one’s eyes and catch a sparrow is to deceive oneself.” If even a trivial thing cannot be won by self-deception, how much less the great matter of birth and death!

[Covering one’s eyes to catch a sparrow] Covering one’s eyes to catch a sparrow, thinking that it will not be seen — a metaphor for deceiving oneself. [Even a trivial thing cannot be won by self-deception; how much less the great matter of birth and death] Catching a sparrow is a trivial matter, and yet it cannot be accomplished through self-deception; how much more the great matter of escaping birth and death — how could that possibly be accomplished through self-deception? [Self-deception] Deceiving oneself. The Primal Vow teaching deceives itself, thinking that by tampering with Master Shandao’s teaching of “unbroken thought brings rebirth” and rewriting it as “recitation of the name necessarily brings rebirth,” one may recite the Buddha’s name a little with a scattered mind in daily life, and then surely be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss at the moment of death.
